content:
To determine the energy difference required to clearly distinguish two quantum states, we use the energy-time uncertainty principle. The natural energy width (uncertainty) of a state with lifetime \(\tau\) is approximately \(\Delta E \approx \frac{\hbar}{\tau}\), where \(\hbar \approx 6.58 \times 10^{-16} \text{ eV·s}\).

For the two states:
- State 1: \(\tau_1 = 10^{-9} \text{ s} \Rightarrow \Delta E_1 \approx \frac{6.58 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-9}} = 6.58 \times 10^{-7} \text{ eV}\)
- State 2: \(\tau_2 = 10^{-8} \text{ s} \Rightarrow \Delta E_2 \approx \frac{6.58 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-8}} = 6.58 \times 10^{-8} \text{ eV}\)

To clearly resolve the two energy levels, their energy difference \(\Delta E\) must be larger than the sum of their uncertainties (or at least the larger uncertainty). The sum is \(\approx 7.24 \times 10^{-7} \text{ eV}\).

Comparing with the options:
- (A) \(10^{-8} \text{ eV}\) (too small)
- (B) \(10^{-4} \text{ eV}\) (much larger than \(10^{-7} \text{ eV}\), so clearly resolvable)
- (C) \(10^{-11} \text{ eV}\) (too small)
- (D) \(10^{-9} \text{ eV}\) (too small)

Only option (B) provides an energy difference large enough to overcome the natural linewidths.

Answer: B
